A new client of mine was compromised a while ago and I jokingly said something about air-gapping their network. Much to my surprise they're actually considering it because of the huge amount of money they just spent on identity protection for their staff. Joy. Myself and /u/e-werd were discussing on IRC a few things relating to "the ultimate network security" and figured it'd be nice for everyone to weigh in.

So, /v/sysadmin, how do you make the absolutely most secure network you know?

Requirements:

  • Obviously users need to do their work and the business needs to make money.
  • You still need a job.
  • Must use computers/servers/networking.

One of the things another local IT guy here does is using software restriction policies to block everything and then just whitelist the apps needed. Things are so locked down in their global environment (100+ sites on 4 continents) that it negates the need for even Antivirus. The desktops are also not allowed to save anything locally and all data must be saved to the network.

He mentioned that even though it took a lot of planning to set up, once done, it was a breeze to manage. He does have to spend some extra time when he gets audited for HIPPA and PCI compliance explaining why there is no endpoint security but he has never had a problem with them once they understand.

I'd be interested to see where/how the policies mitigate against vulnerable/exploitable code, and where in the stack it limits execution them.

Obviously, you still have a risk of insider threat, and spearphishing attacks that could cause Data Loss, too.

I think whats also interesting is signature based black-lists. According to the Verizon Data Breach[1] Investigation Report, roughly 90% of the malware on networks is coded specifically for that network. So, in this case that point is moot, but its an interesting figure to note.

[1]http://www.verizonenterprise.com/DBIR/2015/

Edit: Do they have/monitor IDS/IPS or have a SIEM, or all/some of the above?

I would have to ask. I run the local SpiceCorps meetings here in Las Vegas and this user talked for about 45 min on how he did it. This all stemmed from a conversation on gateway antivirus vs endpoint antivirus and if you need both and/or one.

I agree that spearphishing attacks are one thing that is hard to protect against and that would be where training comes in. I have training a client to email me anything suspicious to verify after they were hit by cryptowall.

I try to work from the black swan perspective: you're never going to be able to prevent attacks but you can minimize or mitigate damage and create robust systems. Netflix is a great example of this idea (although their corporate systems are standard enterprise setup).

But as always... security in layers!

I run SecurityOnion for IDS \ SIEM.

On the network side I route at the access layer and ACL between switches. I run RADIUS and .1x on every port at access plus use port isolation. I don't propagate VLANs so there's very little possibility of ARP spoofs and I record MAC to IP and since every access switch is is own restricted IP range I can easily track physically where a packet originates.

I firewall between my cluster and my end users so only the ports expected are allowed.

At the edge, I use the emergent threats list on my routers for filtering and I firewall in both directions by port and originating IP range. I don't have application aware security at the moment but I with with what I have.

I have all of my internet facing servers behind hardened HAproxy although I could do a better job there
